content:
Who I Am I’m a PhD researcher at Monash University’s ACTION Lab, supervised by Delvin Varghese and Patrick Olivier. My research sits at the intersection of privacy engineering, trusted computing, and human-computer interaction.
Before academia, I spent 5+ years as a software engineer in Seoul, South Korea, building blockchain infrastructure, ZK-rollup systems, and decentralized applications.
Research Focus I’m building Epsilon — a privacy-preserving research infrastructure platform that enables researchers to work with sensitive data while maintaining cryptographic guarantees of execution integrity.
The core idea: instead of trusting institutions to handle your data correctly, we provide verifiable proof that your specific code ran on your specific dataset inside a secure enclave — and nothing else leaked.
Key areas:

content:
Epsilon: Privacy-Preserving Research Infrastructure My PhD research addresses three fundamental problems with how sensitive data is handled in research environments today.
The Problem Trusted Research Environments (TREs) are the standard infrastructure for working with sensitive health, social, and government data. But they have critical limitations:
Problem Current State Impact Data sovereignty Researchers can’t bring their own datasets Limits research scope Manual policy enforcement Weeks of approval delays for each data request Slows research by months No execution verification No proof that code ran correctly on the right data Trust is assumed, not verified My Approach Epsilon integrates four mechanisms that map to the Five Safes framework:
RQ1: Archetypes — Visual Schema Mapping How can adaptive schema abstraction support BYOD environments?
Archetypes are visual, hierarchical schema mappings that let data custodians define exactly what data researchers can access. Instead of flat checkbox lists, custodians build tree structures that make data relationships and sensitivity visible — enabling better data minimization decisions.
Status: Completed and integrated.
RQ2: AI-Assisted Policy Checking How can AI agents reduce manual review bottlenecks?
A multi-agent system (built with CrewAI + GPT-4) that automatically checks whether a researcher’s data request complies with institutional policies. The AI analyzes research purpose, data sensitivity, and proportionality — flagging concerns for human review rather than replacing human judgment.
Status: Proof of concept completed.
RQ3: Per-Execution Cryptographic Verification How can we provide verifiable proof that specific code ran on specific data?
This is the core technical contribution. Current TEE platforms (Phala, dstack) prove: “This application runs in a TEE.” Epsilon extends this to: “Your specific code ran on your specific dataset at this specific time” — using Zero-Knowledge Proofs (Groth16/BN128) combined with AWS Nitro Enclave attestation.
Status: In development (ZKP circuit implementation).
Architecture The full pipeline: Data upload → Archetype configuration → AI policy check → TEE execution → ZKP proof generation → Verifiable output
Built with:
Frontend: React (visual schema mapper) Backend: Python, FastAPI AI: CrewAI framework, OpenAI GPT-4 Security: AWS Nitro Enclaves Cryptography: Circom, SnarkJS, Groth16/BN128 What Makes This Different Existing Systems Epsilon Platform attestation (“app runs in TEE”) Per-execution binding (code + data + timestamp) Top-down access control Participatory visual schema mapping Manual policy review (weeks) AI-augmented review (minutes) Trust the institution Verify cryptographically
